description: Sasquatch is the great hairy wild man of the Pacific Northwest woods, attested across many Indigenous traditions under local names such as Halkomelem sæsq'ec, source of the word 'sasquatch.' Usually a huge, ape-like forest dweller who leaves enormous footprints, he ranges from a dangerous man-eater in some legends to a shy forest guardian in others. Modern Bigfoot sightings keep the legend alive.
source: Etymonline 'sasquatch' (Halkomelem sæsq'ec, 1929); native-americans.com Chinook Legends (Boqs/Skookum); Wikipedia 'Sasquatch'
research_notes: Attested as a genuine Indigenous-derived tradition, though 'Sasquatch (Bigfoot)' is a modern umbrella term. The word 'sasquatch' comes from Halkomelem (Coast Salish) sæsq'ec (Etymonline, first cited 1929); in the Chinook trade area the wild man is called Boqs (also Siatco, Sasquatch or Skookum), usually a dangerous man-eating monster though sometimes benign like the Halkomelem Sasquatch (native-americans.com). The 'USA culture' field is a generic label; the tradition is Pacific Northwest and spans both US and Canadian territory.

description: Gunakadeit, the Tlingit sea wolf or sea monster, is the great being of the outer coast who supplies wealth and food. In the story told at Wrangell, a young man gained Gunakadeit's power by wearing its skin and used it to feed his starving village. Related peoples, including the Tsimshian and Haida, tell of the same marine transformer; its name now labels a fossil sea reptile from southeast Alaska.
source: John R. Swanton, 'Tlingit Myths and Texts' (1909); Katishan of Wrangell account; Wikipedia 'Gunakadeit'
research_notes: Attested as Gunakadeit, the Tlingit sea wolf/sea monster. In Swanton's recorded account the young man of Wrangell acquired the monster's skin and used it to feed his village; the being is known across the Tlingit-Tsimshian-Haida region. The record's 'Haida' fun_fact and generic 'Canada' culture field are loose; the core figure is Tlingit (southeast Alaska/British Columbia). The fossil thalattosaur Gunakadeit joseeae is named after it. 'Sea Bear' is a less common gloss for this sea-monster figure.

description: In Tlingit tradition the sea monster Gunakadeit, the great sea wolf of the outer islands, appears to lone travelers and can be brought ashore only with the right ritual knowledge. Its supernatural skin grants its wearer power to hunt and feed a community. The figure belongs to the wider Northwest Coast belief in powerful undersea beings.
source: John R. Swanton, 'Tlingit Myths and Texts' (1909); Tlingit oral tradition
research_notes: Attested: this 'Sea Monster' record refers to the Tlingit sea-wolf/monster Gunakadeit, the same figure as the separate 'sea-bear' entry. Tlingit territory spans southeast Alaska and British Columbia, so the USA/Canada split of the figure is artificial but not wrong. Note the input's archetype 'forest-spirit' and strengths list are template filler; the being is a marine spirit. Recommend merging with sea-bear.

description: Inuit oral tradition tells of several dangerous marine beings, not one named 'Sea Monsters.' Qalupalik lurks beneath the sea ice and snatches children who wander onto thin ice; Arnapkapfaaluk, 'the terrible woman of the sea,' is a form of the Sea Mother who eats hunters. The record is a category label, and its linked Sinbad story is an error.
source: None — category label; analogues: Qalupalik, Arnapkapfaaluk (Inuit oral tradition); see sedna-greenland record
research_notes: Not attested as a single named being; 'Sea Monsters' is a category. Real Inuit marine monsters include Qalupalik (a humanlike creature that grabs children near open water or holes in the ice) and Arnapkapfaaluk, a child-stealing, man-eating form of the sea deity related to Sedna. The record's stories array references 'sinbad-the-sailor-seven-voyages,' an incorrect cross-reference that should be removed. Culture 'Canada' is fair for Inuit tradition.

description: Sea-serpent traditions are documented along the Northwest Coast, where the great horned water serpent appears in the art and ceremony of several peoples. The Sisiutl of the Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth and Coast Salish is the classic form: a horned serpent with a head at each end and a central human-like face, whose glance can kill, and whose image protects warriors and house fronts.
source: Wikipedia 'Sisiutl'; Roderick Paul Paterson, 'The northwest coast sisiutl' (UBC thesis, 1975); Spirits of the West Coast Gallery
research_notes: Attested as a class, with the Sisiutl as its best-documented representative. The Sisiutl is documented among the Kwakwaka'wakw, Nuu-chah-nulth and Coast Salish (Paterson 1975; contemporary Coast Salish retellings). Seeing it means death for the ordinary person; warriors who approach it gain superhuman strength, and its image is carved on houses and worn for protection (godsandmonsters.info; Spirits of the West Coast). The record's 'Salish' fun_fact is supportable for the regional sea-serpent complex.

description: Sedna is the great sea mother of the Inuit, mistress of the whales, seals and walruses, who lives in Adlivun beneath the ocean. A mortal girl who was thrown from her father's boat, she became the sea animals when her severed fingers were cut away. Hunters keep her favor by obeying taboos; when they fail, the angakkuq (shaman) must journey to comb her hair and free the animals she withholds.
source: native-languages.org Sedna; Canadian Museum of History; 'The Origin of Sedna' (Inuit oral tradition)
research_notes: Attested and central to Inuit religion. Sedna (Sanna, Nuliajuk, Arnakuagsak, Sassuma Arnaa, Takánakapsâluk, 'Old-woman-who-lived-in-the-sea') is the sea goddess and mistress of sea mammals, documented across Arctic regions under many local names and versions. The severed-fingers origin is standard, and the angakkuq's journey to her undersea home to comb her hair and confess communal sins is well documented. Culture 'Canada' is fair; a separate sedna-greenland entry duplicates the same deity.

description: Not independently attested as a USA or North American being. The Olmec were an ancient Mesoamerican civilization of the Gulf Coast of Mexico, and no specific 'Shade' spirit is documented among them; the record's burial-site and battlefield habitat tags are template filler.
source: None — no source for a USA 'Olmec shade'; analogues: Mictlantecuhtli and Mictlan (Aztec/Mesoamerican underworld)
research_notes: Not attested. The Olmec civilization is Mesoamerican (Veracruz and Tabasco, Mexico), not North American/USA, and no 'Shade (Olmec)' being is documented in the literature. The related records shadeolmec-mexico and shadeolmec-colombia suggest the slug was generated by country-spreading a name. Honest analogues are the Mesoamerican underworld (Mictlan) and death deities such as Mictlantecuhtli, though these are Aztec, not specifically Olmec. Recommend country correction to Mexico or removal.

description: The Shalako are tall, ten-foot kachina messengers of the Zuni, beings of great spiritual power who appear each winter. During the Shalako ceremony, six Shalako—each the horned, feathered impersonation of a rain-bringing spirit—visit the newly built ceremonial houses, blessing the homes and the people.
source: Ruth Bunzel, 'Zuñi Ceremonialism' (1932); native-languages.org Zuni Legends; Zuni Pueblo tradition
research_notes: Attested. The Shalako are genuine Zuni kachina messengers and the annual Shalako ceremony is among the most famous Zuni ceremonies: six Shalako visit newly built homes each winter, associated with the Sayatasha rain society (Bunzel). The record's culture field 'USA' should be corrected to Zuni Pueblo. Its fun_fact 'Hopi tradition' is wrong — Shalako is Zuni, not Hopi. The Hopi analogue would be their own kachina messengers generally.

description: Shamans are ritual practitioners, not spirits: among the Tlingit the shaman (íx̲t) gained power from spirit helpers to heal, find lost souls and combat witchcraft; among the Inuit the angakkuq serves the community and speaks with the sea mother Sedna. The record uses 'Shaman' as a generic spirit entry; the genuine figure is the human medicine person of each nation's tradition.
source: Tlingit tradition (íx̲t); Knud Rasmussen, 'Intellectual Culture of the Iglulik Eskimos' (angakkuq)
research_notes: Semi-attested as a category: shamanism is real, but the record's type 'spirit' is a category error — the shaman is a human practitioner. The Tlingit shaman (íx̲t) worked through spirit helpers; the Inuit angakkuq is the community healer who journeys to Sedna. The linked stories 'tiggak-the-shaman' and 'the-bewitchment-of-angutisugsuk' are Inuit, supporting a northern attribution. Recommend retyping as a practitioner/role rather than a spirit being.

description: In Miwok creation stories Silver Fox is a wise creator being who, working with Coyote, shaped the world. Depending on the telling Silver Fox is female or male, but always the quiet, deliberate partner to Coyote's impulsiveness: together they sang and danced the earth into being. Silver Fox appears across northern and central California traditions as a culture hero and a being of the early world.
source: Joseph Bruchac, 'Native American Stories'; Miwok oral tradition (Pomo, Coast Miwok variants)
research_notes: Attested. The Miwok creation account features Silver Fox (female in the most commonly retold version) and Coyote, who together create the world (Bruchac). In some northern Californian traditions, such as the Achumawi, the creator is a male Silver Fox. The record's 'USA' culture field is generic; the correct attribution is Miwok (California). Its 'forest-spirit' archetype is a loose gloss — Silver Fox is a creator being of the primordial world.

description: Sinti is the Great Serpent of Choctaw tradition, a water monster with a panther's head and horns that dwells in rivers, lakes and whirlpools. One of the three great spirits alongside the creator and the Raven, Sinti is the dangerous being who can overturn canoes and drag people under. He is both feared and honored, with offerings made to keep his waters calm.
source: native-languages.org Choctaw Legends; H.S. Halbert, 'The Choctaw Creation Legend'; Access Genealogy
research_notes: Attested. Sinti is the Choctaw Great Serpent, a two-horned, panther-headed water monster and one of the three great spirits of Choctaw lore (with the creator and the Raven). The record's source line citing 'Lakota Sinte' is wrong — that is a different word (Sinte is Lakota for 'tail,' as in the name Sinte Gleska). Correct attribution is Choctaw. The linked story 'the-legend-of-lake-titicaca' is an unrelated, incorrect cross-reference.

description: The Sisiutl is the double-headed sea serpent of the Kwakwaka'wakw and neighboring Northwest Coast peoples, with a serpent head at each end of its body and a human-like face at the centre, all three horned. Seeing it means death to the unprepared, but a warrior who faces it may gain superhuman strength and armor from its blood and hide. Its image guards houses, canoes and warriors.
source: Wikipedia 'Sisiutl'; Roderick Paul Paterson, 'The northwest coast sisiutl' (UBC, 1975); godsandmonsters.info
research_notes: Attested. The Sisiutl is the Kwakwaka'wakw double-headed (three-faced, three-horned) sea serpent, documented in art and ceremony across the Northwest Coast, including Nuu-chah-nulth and Coast Salish peoples (Paterson 1975). Its slime trail is lethal and the warrior's power gained from its blood is well documented (godsandmonsters.info). Record culture 'Canada' is fair (Kwakwaka'wakw live in British Columbia); its 'Haida' fun_fact is imprecise — the core attribution is Kwakwaka'wakw.

description: Skadegamutc is the ghost-witch of Wabanaki (Abenaki) tradition, the malevolent spirit of a sorcerer who died unquiet. It can change its shape, appearing as a human, a shadow, or an animal, and drifts along forest paths or into villages after sunset, watching unseen. It represents dangerous spiritual power and the warning against misuse of magic.
source: native-languages.org Wabanaki Legends; Abenaki oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as documented on native-languages.org and in Abenaki/Wabanaki tradition: the skadegamutc is the undead ghost-witch able to shift between human, animal and shadow forms, wandering villages and forest paths after dark and observing while unseen. It is a cautionary figure about the misuse of spiritual power. The record's culture 'United States' is fair for the Wabanaki (Maine), though the Abenaki also live in Quebec and New Brunswick (Canada).

description: Yee naaldlooshii, 'by means of it, it goes on all fours,' is the Navajo term for a harmful witch who can turn into, possess, or disguise itself as an animal, typically by wearing the animal's skin. Skinwalkers are one kind of 'ánti'įhnii, a person who practices evil, the antithesis of Navajo healing values, and are blamed for illness, death and misfortune.
source: Wikipedia 'Skin-walker'; Clyde Kluckhohn, 'Navaho Witchcraft' (1944)
research_notes: Attested and culturally sensitive. Yee naaldlooshii (skin-walker) is the Navajo harmful witch who changes form by putting on an animal's skin; it is a class of 'ánti'įhnii witch, opposed to Navajo values, and a taboo subject seldom discussed with outsiders (Wikipedia; Kluckhohn 1944). Common forms are wolf, coyote and owl. Note: the 'silver' and 'true name' weaknesses in the input are pop-culture additions, not Navajo lore. Culture field 'Navajo Nation' is correct. Handle respectfully and avoid sensationalizing.

description: Skookum, from Chinook Jargon meaning 'strong' or 'powerful,' names the mountain giants and evil spirits of Pacific Northwest tradition. In Chinook folklore the wild man of the woods, called Boqs, Siatco, Sasquatch or Skookum, is a large, hairy forest being, usually a dangerous man-eater though sometimes benign.
source: Wikipedia 'Skookum'; native-americans.com Chinook Legends (Boqs); Cascadia Bioregion, Chinook Wawa word of the day
research_notes: Attested. 'Skookum' is Chinook Jargon for 'strong/powerful,' from Lower Chehalis skúkum 'ghost, spirit, monster'; as a being it denotes the Pacific Northwest mountain giant or wild man (the same class as Sasquatch, also called Boqs in Chinook tradition) and evil spirits represented by birds and beasts that could inhabit people and cause serious illness (Wikipedia; Cascadia Bioregion). The input's 'steals children, helps hunters, communicates by drumming' details are embellishments; the core giant-and-spirit tradition is real. Attribution: Chinook trade area of the Pacific Northwest.

description: The Cheyenne creator Maheo, also called Heammawihio, 'the one who lives above,' is the supreme being who made the world from the void, molding the earth brought by a diving duck into the land. He is a spirit without human form, rarely personified, and in some tellings he first made people immortal before changing death to its present form.
source: George Bird Grinnell, 'By Cheyenne Campfires' and 'The Cheyenne Indians'; native-languages.org Maheo
research_notes: Attested. The Cheyenne supreme being is Maheo (Ma'heo'o), also rendered Heammawihio ('Wise One Above' per one source; 'Spider Above' per native-languages.org), a creator without human form, rarely personified, who made the earth from a bit of mud brought up by a diving duck or coot (native-languages.org; Grinnell). He is paired with a 'Wise One Below.' The record's 'water-spirit' archetype and 'aquatic speed' strengths are template errors; this is a creator sky god. 'Sky Father' is a fair gloss, though Cheyenne tradition rarely genders or personifies Maheo.

description: The Sky People are the celestial beings of the upper world in Blackfoot tradition, the Sspommitapiiksi, the sacred family above the earth: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the star children, foremost Iipisowaahs the Morning Star, who married a mortal and fathered the hero Star-Boy. Sky beings across many peoples descend to teach, marry mortals, and return to homes among the stars.
source: native-languages.org Blackfoot Legends; Clark Wissler & D.C. Duvall, 'Mythology of the Blackfoot Indians' (1908)
research_notes: Attested as the Blackfoot Sspommitapiiksi (Sky Beings/Above People): Naato'si (Sun), Ko'komiki'somm (Moon) and the star children, especially Iipisowaahs (Morning Star), father of the hero Star-Boy (native-languages.org; Wissler & Duvall 1908). The name 'Sky People' also labels analogous sky-dwelling beings in other tribes (the Iroquois Sky Woman motif, etc.), so the record is partly a category. Culture 'USA' should be Blackfoot.

description: 'Spirit Beings' is a general term, not a single attested figure: in Salish and other Northwest Coast traditions the world is inhabited by countless spirits dwelling in rocks, trees, waters and winds. These beings must be treated with respect and given offerings, and they can help or harm people depending on how they are treated. The record names no specific spirit.
source: None — generic label; analogues: Salish spirit-beings complex (native-americans.com Salish legends)
research_notes: Not attested as a single named being; it is a category. Coast Salish cosmology does hold that natural places are inhabited by spirits that must be respected, so the framing is fair, but no specific entity named 'Spirit Beings' exists. Recommend either pointing to a concrete being (e.g., a named Salish water or sky spirit) or marking as a category as done here. The 'Salish tradition' fun_fact is a reasonable regional attribution for the general concept.

description: Standing Rock, the stone formation on the Missouri in what is now North Dakota, is a petrified human in Lakota tradition: a young woman turned to stone, in some tellings a jealous Dakota wife. The Arikara, who also lived at the site, told of the Great Spirit turning a woman to rock. The landmark later became a symbol of Indigenous water-rights protests.
source: Wikipedia 'Standing Rock'; North Dakota oral tradition (Lakota/Dakota and Arikara)
research_notes: Attested as a place-legend. The Standing Rock is the petrified body of a woman in the Lakota account (a jealous Dakota wife turned to stone for her betrayal); the Arikara variant tells of the Great Spirit petrifying a woman to protect her. Both are recorded versions of the site-name legend. The record's 'Kiowa tradition' fun_fact is wrong — the tradition is Lakota/Dakota and Arikara. The 2016 protest association is a recent development, not part of the origin legend.

description: The Stick Indians, also called Cheeplokkeeycum, are malevolent forest spirits of the Salish, Lummi, Yakama and Cayuse peoples of the Pacific Northwest, luring travelers astray with whistles and laughter and capable of paralyzing or harming them. Salish tellers describe them as large, hairy wild men, others as forest dwarves. 'Stick Indians' is an English euphemism for a taboo name.
source: native-languages.org Stick Indians; Salish and Plateau oral tradition
research_notes: Attested as the Pacific Northwest 'Stick Indians' (Cheeplokkeeycum), documented among the Salish, Lummi, Yakama and Cayuse: malevolent forest spirits that imitate human voices and whistling, lead people astray, and can cause paralysis, confusion or harm; 'Stick Indians' is a euphemism for a taboo name (native-languages.org). The record's 'Creek tradition' attribution is unsupported — no Creek/Muscogee 'Stick People' figure was found in Creek folklore sources; this is the Plateau/Northwest complex. Recommend correcting the culture field to Salish/Plateau.

description: Not attested as a Pueblo being. The name 'Stihi' is Albanian, naming a fire-breathing storm demon related to the kulshedra, and no 'Stihi/Stihini' giant appears in Pueblo or New Mexico folklore. The closest real Pueblo giant is Tsahveeyo of the Tewa, a huge being who dwelt on a mesa and preyed on children in the pueblos. The record appears to be a fabricated or mislabeled entry.
source: None — no Pueblo source; the word is Albanian (Wikipedia 'Stihi'; Elsie, 'A Dictionary of Albanian Religion, Mythology and Folk Culture'). Real analogue: Tsahveeyo (Tewa Pueblo giant)
research_notes: Not attested. Searches found no Pueblo or Native American 'Stihi/Stihini'; the name is Albanian, a storm and treasure-guarding dragon demon related to the kulshedra (Wikipedia 'Stihi'; Elsie 2001). The record's 'Pueblo giant from New Mexico' habitat of mesas and cliff dwellings likely derives from the Tewa tradition of Tsahveeyo, a giant who lived on a mesa and preyed on children in the pueblos (New Mexican Folklore archive). The input's source line conflates the record with 'Stick Indians.' Marked unattested; recommend replacing with Tsahveeyo or deleting.

description: The Stone Coats, or stone giants, are terrible giants of Iroquois tradition, taller than any man and covered in a skin of rock-hard scales (native names include Genonsgwa). They wander the winter lands of the Adirondacks and Alleghenies, and heroes defeat them by striking their one soft spot.
source: native-languages.org Iroquois Legends (Stone Giants); Arthur C. Parker, 'Seneca Myths and Folk Tales'
research_notes: Attested. The Iroquois (Haudenosaunee) stone giants, known as Genonsgwa (Gennonsgwa/Genonskwa) with other local variants including Strendu, are covered in rock-hard scales, about twice as tall as a human, and associated with the cold north and winter; heroes slay them by striking the one weak spot (native-languages.org; Parker). Parallel figures: Cherokee Stoneclad, Abenaki Giwakwa, Ojibwe Windigo, Mi'kmaq Jenu, Cree Witiko. The record's 'Piasa variant' framing is inaccurate; Stone Coat is not the Piasa. The linked Cherokee story is about the parallel Nu'nu'yi, not the Iroquois figure.

description: Muisca tradition pairs the Moon goddess Chía with Sué (also Sua), the masculine Sun god, both born from the creator Chiminigagua. The zipa of Bacatá claimed descent from Sué's lineage, and the Sun was worshipped with offerings at sacred sites of the Colombian highlands. Modern summaries that call the Sun a 'goddess' likely conflate Sué with Chía; Muisca belongs to Colombia, not the USA.
source: Wikipedia 'Muisca mythology'; Colombian highland (Altiplano Cundiboyacense) oral tradition
research_notes: Correction needed. In Muisca (Chibcha) mythology the Sun deity is masculine — Sué/Sua — while Chía is the Moon goddess; both derive from the creator Chiminigagua, and the Bacatá zipa traced descent from Sué (Wikipedia Muisca mythology). 'Sun Goddess (Muisca)' is therefore a mislabel: the record either refers to Sué (male sun god) or to Chía (moon goddess). The country field 'USA' is wrong — the Muisca are the peoples of the Colombian highlands (see also the sungoddessmuisca-colombia record). Describe Sué and note the gender discrepancy.

description: The sweat house is a central institution of Yurok life: an earth-covered plank building in every village where men gathered daily, slept and prepared for ceremonies. Heated by fire rather than steam, it was the assembly place of the men and the setting of prayers and purification before the world-renewing dances such as the Deerskin and Brush dances.
source: A.L. Kroeber, 'Elements of Culture in Native California' (1922); Yurok Tribe ceremonial water materials
research_notes: Attested, though as an institution rather than a spirit. The Yurok sweat house (part of the northwestern California complex described by Kroeber) was an earth-covered structure used daily by the men, heated by fire rather than steam, never admitting women except on special ceremonial occasions, and central to ceremonial purification; Yurok ceremonial practices require sweathouses near clean bathing water (Kroeber; Yurok Tribe). The record's 'spirit' framing is a category error; it is a ritual structure.

description: In Greenland, Sedna is known by many names — Arnakuagsak, Arnaqquassaaq, Sassuma Arnaa — the great sea mother who lives at the bottom of the ocean and owns the whales, seals and walruses. She was a mortal girl whose severed fingers became the sea mammals after her father betrayed her.
source: native-languages.org Sedna; Greenland Inuit oral tradition
research_notes: Attested; this is the Greenlandic variant of the same deity as the sedna (Canada) record. Greenland names: Arnakuagsak/Arnaqquassaaq, Sassuma Arnaa (West Greenland); Takánakapsâluk (Igloolik); Nuliajuk (Kivalliq). The core story — betrayal, severed fingers becoming sea mammals, the shaman's underwater journey to comb her hair — is consistent across regions. The relatedNames 'Qailertetang' is a second, distinct Inuit sea goddess: related but not the same being. This entry duplicates the sedna record.

description: The Siagtut (Siasgiut) are lost hunters of Greenland Inuit tradition who froze to death on the Arctic ice and whose souls were placed in the sky, where they now shine as the three stars of Orion's Belt. They serve as an eternal warning to hunters about the dangers of the wilderness, and travelers use the belt to keep their bearings. They can only watch, fixed forever in the night sky.
source: Greenland Inuit oral tradition; Mythfolks 'The Lost Hunters of Orion'
research_notes: Attested in Greenland Inuit star-lore: the three stars of Orion's Belt are the Siasgiut/Siaqtut, hunters who became lost on the ice and were set in the sky as a warning, and the asterism is used for navigation. Reasonably documented (Mythfolks; Greenland tradition); the record's 'good' source quality is fair. Note the spelling: the research literature gives 'Siasgiut,' while the slug uses 'Siagtut' — same being. Behavior tags 'observing, warning' and motif of immobility fit the fixed-in-the-sky account.

description: Jóhonaaʼéí, the Sun, is a central deity of the Navajo (Diné). A being in human form, he carries the Sun across the sky each day and hangs it on a peg in his home at night. He is the father, with Changing Woman (Asdzą́ą́ Nádleehé), of the hero twins Nayééneizghani (Monster Slayer) and Tóbájíshchíní (Child of the Water), the slayers of the monsters of the old world.
source: Washington Matthews, 'Navaho Legends' (1897); Zolbrod, 'Diné bahaneʼ'; Navajo ceremonial tradition
research_notes: Attested. Jóhonaaʼéí (also rendered Tsohanoai in older literature) is the Navajo Sun deity, father of the Hero Twins who rid the world of the monsters; the account of him carrying the Sun across the sky and hanging it on a peg in his house at night is recorded in Navajo origin narratives (Matthews; windows2universe; mythlok). The input's description and summary accidentally pasted text about Changing Woman from another record — that was a template error; the corrected content describes the Sun himself. Culture 'Navajo' is correct.

description: In the Hopi story told by Harold Courlander, the boy Sikakokuh owns an extraordinary hunting dog that is no ordinary animal: it tracks game without fail, warns its master of danger, and seems to understand human speech. The tale, 'Sikakokuh and the hunting dog,' shows the dog acting as a spirit helper and guardian, an example of the animal helpers common in Pueblo oral tradition.
source: Harold Courlander, 'People of the Short Blue Corn: Tales and Legends of the Hopi Indians' (1970)
research_notes: Attested to a specific literary source: the tale 'Sikakokuh and the hunting dog' appears in Harold Courlander's 1970 collection 'People of the Short Blue Corn,' a retelling of Hopi tradition (the linked story 'sikakokuh-and-the-hunting-dog' confirms the chapter exists). The dog is a story-specific spirit helper with supernatural tracking and communication, not an independently circulated being, so it is best treated as a tale figure. Culture 'Hopi' is correct.
